summary: This best current practice specifies tests to check whether independent implementations of a performance metric RFC agree, like an interoperability test for metrics. Results are gathered under the same conditions and compared statistically.

plainLanguage.summary:
Most standards advance by showing that two separate implementations can work together. A performance metric is different, because a measurement tool does not exchange anything with another measurement tool; it only measures the network.

So this RFC defines a different kind of proof. Two independent implementations are measured against the same network at the same time, and their results are compared statistically. If two systems that should be measuring the same thing produce the same numbers, then the metric definition must be clear enough for both to read it the same way, and the metric RFC is fit to advance.

subtitle: How to show that two independent implementations of a performance metric measure the same thing.

tldr.problem: A protocol advances when two implementations are shown to talk to each other. A performance metric cannot do that: the measurement systems never exchange packets with each other, so nothing about their behaviour is observable from outside.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines interoperability for a metric as producing statistically equivalent results under the same network conditions. It requires each implementation to be tested against the specification on its own, a test setup that makes the path and the conditions identical, and a statistical comparison of the results.
tldr.outcome: A metric RFC can be assessed for clarity rather than for protocol compatibility, and options that nobody implemented can be removed. The document updates RFC 2026 with the tests that apply to metric specifications.

today: RFC 6576 is a Best Current Practice that has not been obsoleted. It updates RFC 2026, adding the tests that apply when the specification being advanced is a performance metric rather than a protocol.

sections.title: Why a Metric Needs Its Own Test
sections.content:
The Internet Standards Process as updated by RFC 6410 specifies that widespread deployment and use is sufficient to show interoperability as a condition for advancement to Internet Standard. The previous requirement of interoperability tests prior to advancing an RFC to the Standard maturity level, specified in RFC 2026 and RFC 5657, has been removed. While the modified requirement is applicable to protocols, wide deployment of different measurement systems does not prove that the implementations measure metrics in a standard way. Section 5.3 of RFC 5657 explicitly mentions the special case of standards that are not on-the-wire protocols. This document takes the position that flexible metric definitions can be proven to be clear and unambiguous through tests that compare the results from independent implementations.

It describes tests that infer whether metric specifications are sufficient using a definition of metric interoperability: measuring equivalent results, in a statistical sense, under the same network conditions.

For a protocol specification the notion of interoperability is reasonably intuitive, since the implementations must successfully talk to each other while exercising all features and options, and to achieve interoperability two implementors need to interpret the protocol specifications in equivalent ways. In the case of IP Performance Metrics, that definition is only useful for test and control protocols such as the One-Way Active Measurement Protocol and the Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol. A metric specification RFC describes one or more metric definitions, methods of measurement and a way to report the results of measurement, for example a way to test and report the one-way delay that data packets incur while being sent from one network location to another.

Since many implementations of IP metrics are embedded in measurement systems that do not interact with one another, having been built before OWAMP and TWAMP, the interoperability evaluation cannot be determined by observing that independent implementations interact properly for various protocol exchanges. Instead, verifying that different implementations give statistically equivalent results under controlled measurement conditions takes the place of interoperability observations.

The Standards advancement process aims at producing confidence that the metric definitions and supporting material are clearly worded and unambiguous, or at revealing ways in which the metric definitions can be revised to achieve clarity. It also permits identification of options that were not implemented, so that they can be removed from the advancing specification. The product of the process is therefore information about the metric specification RFC itself: which definitions are clear and unambiguous and which are not, as opposed to an evaluation of the implementations that assist in the process.

The metric RFC advancement process begins with a request for protocol action accompanied by a memo that documents the supporting tests and results. The procedures of RFC 2026 are expanded in RFC 5657, including sample implementation and interoperability reports.
sections.plainLanguage: Protocols prove themselves by talking to each other. Metrics cannot, because a measurement tool never talks to another one. This RFC replaces that with a statistical comparison and puts the burden of proof on the wording of the metric definition instead.

sections.title: The Basic Idea
sections.content:
The implementation of a standard compliant metric is expected to meet the requirements of the related metric specification, so before comparing two metric implementations each one is individually compared against the metric specification.

Most metric specifications leave freedom to implementors on non-fundamental aspects of an individual metric or its options. Comparing different measurement results using a statistical test with the assumption of identical test path and testing conditions requires knowledge of all differences in the overall test setup. Metric specification options chosen by implementors have to be documented, and it is RECOMMENDED to use identical metric options for any test proposed here, with the exception of a variable parameter of the metric definition that is not configurable in one or more implementations. Calibrations specified by metric standards SHOULD be performed to further identify and possibly reduce potential sources of error in the test setup.

The IPPM Framework expects that a methodology for a metric should have the property that it is repeatable: if the methodology is used multiple times under identical conditions, it should result in consistent measurements. An implementation is therefore expected to repeatedly measure a metric with consistent results, and small deviations in the test setup are expected to lead to small deviations in results only. To characterize statistical equivalence in the case of small deviations, RFC 2330 and RFC 2679 suggest applying a 95% confidence interval, chosen because a particular confidence level should be specified so that the results of independent implementations can be compared.

Two different implementations are expected to produce statistically equivalent results if they both measure a metric under the same networking conditions. In statistical terms, separate metric implementations collect separate samples from the same underlying statistical process, and the hypothesis to be tested is that both samples do not expose statistically different properties. This requires careful test design.

The measurement test setup must be self-consistent to the largest possible extent: network conditions and paths MUST be identical for the compared implementations to the largest possible degree, including both the stability and non-ambiguity of the routes taken by the measurement packets. Metric implementations SHOULD use identical options and parameters for the metric under evaluation, to minimize the influence of implementation options on the result. The sample size must be large enough to minimize its influence on the consistency of the test results, which may be especially important if two implementations measure with different average packet transmission rates, and the implementation with the lowest average packet transmission rate determines the smallest temporal interval for which samples can be compared. Comparisons should be repeated with several independent metric samples, to avoid random indications of compatibility or the lack of it.

The document does not propose to base interoperability indications on comparisons of individual singletons, since individual singletons may be impacted by many statistical effects while they are measured, and comparing two singletons of different implementations may result in failures with higher probability than comparing samples.
sections.plainLanguage: Two systems are judged equivalent if their numbers come from the same underlying distribution, measured over the same network at the same time. That means the test path must be the same, the settings must be the same, the sample must be big enough, and the comparison must be repeated rather than done once.

sections.title: Testing One Implementation Against the Specification
sections.content:
A metric implementation is compliant with a metric specification if it supports the requirements classified as MUST and REQUIRED in the related metric specification. An implementation that implements all requirements is fully compliant with the specification, and the degree of compliance SHOULD be noted in the conclusions of the report.

Supported options of a metric implementation SHOULD be documented in sufficient detail to evaluate whether the specification was correctly interpreted. The documentation of chosen options should minimize and recognize differences in the test setup if two implementations are compared, and is used to validate or clarify the wording of a metric specification option, and to remove options that saw no implementation or that are badly specified from the metric specification. This documentation SHOULD be included for all implementation-relevant parts of a metric picked for a comparison, even those not explicitly marked as MUST or REQUIRED in the RFC text. This applies to the Singleton Definition of the Metric, the Sample Definition of the Metric, the Statistics Definition of the Metric, the timing and synchronization-related specification if relevant for the metric, and any other technical part present or missing in the metric specification that is relevant for implementing it.

RFC 2330 and RFC 2679 emphasize precision as an aim of IPPM metric implementations, and a single IPPM-conforming implementation should under otherwise identical network conditions produce precise results for repeated measurements of the same metric. RFC 2330 prefers the empirical distribution function to describe collections of measurements, and determines that unless otherwise stated IPPM goodness-of-fit tests are done using 5% significance. The goodness-of-fit test determines by which precision two or more samples of a metric implementation belong to the same underlying distribution. The test suggested here is the Anderson-Darling K-sample test, where K stands for the number of samples to be compared.

The results of a repeated test with a single implementation MUST pass an Anderson-Darling K-sample test with a confidence level of 95%. The conditions for which the test has been passed with the specified confidence level MUST be documented. Put another way, the requirement is to document the set of parameters with the smallest deviation at which the results of the tested implementation pass the test, and the minimum resolution available in the reported results from each implementation MUST be taken into account. The documented conditions include the metric resolution at which a test was passed, for example the resolution of timestamps, the parameters modified by an impairment generator, and the impairment generator parameter settings.
sections.plainLanguage: Each implementation is checked on its own first, against the requirements in the metric RFC, and it is tested repeatedly to see how precisely it can repeat itself. That precision is the yardstick: it sets the limit on how different two implementations are allowed to look.

sections.title: Making the Network Conditions the Same
sections.content:
Two major issues complicate tests for metric compliance across live networks under identical testing conditions. One is that metric definition implementations cannot be conveniently examined in field measurement scenarios. The other is described as parallelism in devices and networks, including mechanisms such as those that achieve load balancing. This section proposes two measures to deal with both issues: tunneling mechanisms can be used to avoid parallel processing of different flows in the network, and measuring by separate parallel probe flows results in repeated collection of data. If both measures are combined, wide area network conditions are identical for a number of independent measurement flows, no matter what the network conditions are in detail.

Any measurement setup must avoid the probing traffic itself impeding the metric measurement. The created measurement load must not result in congestion at the access link connecting the measurement implementation to the wide area network, and must not overload the measurement implementation itself, for example by causing a high CPU load or timestamp imprecision due to unwanted queuing while transmitting or receiving test packets.

Tunneling multiple flows destined for a single physical port of a network element allows transmission of all packets via the same path. An existing IP-in-IP tunnel protocol can be applied to avoid Equal-Cost Multi-Path routing of different measurement streams if it meets several criteria: inner IP packets from different measurement implementations are mapped into a single tunnel with a single outer IP origin and destination address, and origin and destination port numbers that are identical for all packets; an easily accessible tunneling protocol allows a metric test to be carried out from more test sites; a low operational overhead may enable a broader audience to set up a metric test; the protocol should be reliable and stable in setup and operation; and it should not incur any extra cost for those interested in setting up a metric test.

If tunneling is applied, two tunnels MUST carry all test traffic between the test site and the remote site. The IP packet size of the metric implementation SHOULD be chosen small enough to avoid fragmentation due to the added Ethernet and tunnel headers. Otherwise the impact of tunnel overhead on fragmentation and interface MTU size must be understood and taken into account.

The following headers may have to be accounted for when calculating total packet length if VLANs and Ethernet over L2TPv3 tunnels are applied: Ethernet 802.1Q at 22 bytes, the L2TPv3 header at 4 to 16 bytes for L2TPv3 data messages over IP and 16 to 28 bytes for L2TPv3 data messages over UDP, the outer IPv4 header at 20 bytes, and MPLS labels, each of which has a length of 4 bytes, of which between 1 and 4 seems a fair expectation. If L2TPv3 is applied, software-based implementations are not suitable for the test setup, as such implementations may cause incalculable delay shifts. Ethernet pseudowires may also be set up on MPLS networks, but MPLS interfaces are mostly found in the network provider domain, so not all of the criteria for selecting a tunneling protocol are met. Setting up a metric test environment is not a plug-and-play issue, and skilled networking engineers should be consulted and involved if a setup between remote sites is preferred.
sections.plainLanguage: Two systems can only be compared if they travel the same path, so the test setup forces every probe packet through the same tunnel. The cost is that headers are added, which the testers have to account for, and that setting this up needs networking expertise rather than a plug.

sections.title: Comparing Two Implementations
sections.content:
RFC 2330 expects that a methodology for a given metric exhibits continuity: for small variations in conditions it results in small variations in the resulting measurements. In the context of the metric test proposed here, a small variation in conditions can be seen as different implementations measuring the same metric along the same path.

IPPM metric specifications, however, allow for implementor options to the largest possible degree, and it cannot be expected that two implementors allow 100% identical options in their implementations. Testers SHOULD pick the same metric measurement configurations for their systems when comparing their implementations by a metric test.

In some cases a goodness-of-fit test may not be possible or may show disappointing results. To clarify the difficulties arising from different metric implementation options, the individual options picked for every compared metric implementation should be documented as specified in the report. If the cause of the failure is a lack of specification clarity, or multiple legitimate interpretations of the definition text, the text should be modified and the resulting memo proposed for consensus and possible advancement to Internet Standard.

The same statistical test as applicable to quantify precision of a single metric implementation must be used to compare metric result equivalence for different implementations. To document compatibility, the smallest measurement resolution at which the compared implementations passed the Anderson-Darling K-sample test must be documented. For different implementations of the same metric, variations in conditions are reasonably expected, so the test comparing samples of the different implementations may result in a lower precision than the test for precision in the same-implementation comparison.
sections.plainLanguage: When the two sets of numbers do not match, the first question is whether the two systems were even configured the same way. If they were, the metric wording is the suspect, and the RFC says to fix the wording and re-run.

sections.title: Clock Synchronization
sections.content:
Clock synchronization effects require special attention. Accuracy of one-way active delay measurements for any metric implementation depends on clock synchronization between the source and destination of tests. Ideally, one-way active delay measurement test endpoints either have direct access to independent GPS or CDMA-based time sources or indirect access to nearby NTP primary, that is stratum 1, time sources equipped with GPS receivers. Access to these time sources may not be available at all test locations associated with different Internet paths.

When secondary, stratum 2 and above, time sources are used with NTP running across the same network whose metrics are subject to comparative implementation tests, network impairments can affect clock synchronization and distort sample one-way values and their interval statistics. Discarding sample one-way delay values for any implementation is recommended when one of two reliability conditions is met: delay is measured and is finite in one direction but not the other; or the absolute value of the difference between the sum of one-way measurements in both directions and the round-trip measurement is greater than X% of the latter value. Examination of the second condition requires round-trip time measurement for reference, for example based on TWAMP in conjunction with one-way delay measurement. Specification of X% to strike a balance between identification of unreliable one-way delay samples and misidentification of reliable samples across a wide range of Internet path round-trip times requires further study.

An IPPM-compliant metric implementation of an RFC that requires synchronized clocks is expected to provide precise measurement results. If an implementation publishes a specification of its precision, such as a precision of 1 ms with plus or minus 500 us and a confidence of 95%, then the specification should be met over a useful measurement duration. For example, if the metric is measured along an Internet path that is stable and not congested, then the precision specification should be met over durations of an hour or more.
sections.plainLanguage: A one-way delay measurement subtracts one clock from another, so clock errors land straight in the result. The RFC says to drop samples where the two directions do not add up to the round trip, and to keep the time sources as close to the real thing as the test sites allow.

sections.title: The Verification Process and the Report
sections.content:
In order to meet their obligations under the IETF Standards Process, the IESG must be convinced that each metric specification advanced to Internet Standard status is clearly written, that there are a sufficient number of verified equivalent implementations, and that options that have been implemented are documented. Each metric, statistic or option of those to be validated MUST be compared against a reference measurement or another implementation as specified in the document.

If two or more implementations do not measure an equivalent metric, and sources of measurement error do not adequately explain the lack of agreement, then the details of each implementation should be audited along with the exact definition text, to determine whether a lack of clarity has caused the implementations to vary in a way that affects the correspondence of the results. If there was a lack of clarity, or multiple legitimate interpretations of the definition text, then the text should be modified and the resulting memo proposed for consensus and possible advancement along the Standards Track.

Any recommendation for the advancement of a metric specification MUST be accompanied by an implementation report, which needs to include the tests performed, the applied test setup, the specific metrics in the RFC, and reports of the tests performed with two or more implementations. The test plan needs to specify the precision reached for each measured metric and thus define the meaning of statistically equivalent for the specific metrics being tested. Ideally, the test plan would co-evolve with the development of the metric, since that is when participants have the clearest context in their minds regarding the different subtleties that can arise.

The implementation report MUST include at minimum: the metric compared and the RFC specifying it, including the statements required by the tests of an individual implementation; the measurement configuration and setup; a complete specification of the measurement stream, meaning the mean rate, the statistical distribution of packets, the packet size or mean packet size and their distribution, the Differentiated Services Code Point, and any other measurement stream properties that could result in deviating results; the duration of each measurement, the number of measurement points collected for each metric during each measurement interval, that is the probe size, and the level of confidence derived from this probe size; the result of the statistical tests performed for each metric validation; a parameterization of laboratory conditions and applied traffic and network conditions allowing reproduction of those conditions for readers; and the documentation helping to improve metric specifications.

All of the tests for each set SHOULD be run in a test setup resulting in identical live network testing conditions. If a different test setup is chosen, it is recommended to avoid effects falsifying results caused by real data networks, such as parallelism in devices and networks. Data networks may forward packets differently when different packet sizes are chosen, when different IP addresses and ports are used and Equal-Cost Multi-Path routing is in operation, when IP options differ, when the DSCP differs, or when the measurements are captured sequentially rather than simultaneously, in which case time varying paths and load conditions come into play.

Section 3.6 of the document proposes a way to set the threshold for equivalence. Each metric is tested by two or more implementations, and each metric is also tested twice simultaneously by the same implementation, using different source and destination address pairs and other differences, so that the connectivity differences of the cross-implementation tests are also experienced and measured by the same implementation. Comparative results for the same implementation represent a bound on cross-implementation equivalence, which is particularly useful when the metric does not produce a continuous distribution of singleton values, such as with a loss metric or a duplication metric. The conclusion is that the implementation with the largest difference in homogeneous comparison results is the lower bound on the equivalence threshold, noting that there may be other systematic errors to account for when comparing implementations. Thus, when evaluating equivalence in cross-implementation results, Maximum_Error = Same_Implementation_Error + Systematic_Error, and only the systematic error need be decided beforehand. Appendix B discusses two ways to perform the analysis, using the R statistical language with its ADK package, and C++ code.
sections.plainLanguage: The process is: measure the same thing with two systems, see whether the numbers agree, and if they do not, check whether the wording of the metric is at fault. The report has to say enough that someone else could repeat the test.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo does not raise any specific security issues. The concerns it does state about the test process are about the load the probes place on the access link and on the measurement implementation, and about keeping the test path stable, rather than about attacks on the testing itself.
sections.plainLanguage: The document adds no security rules of its own. It worries about the test load and about the path staying the same, not about attacks.

viz.caption: THE FIVE WAYS TO RUN THE COMPARISON

items.title: One lab, emulated network
items.text: Both implementations in the same lab with an impairment generator standing in for the Internet.

items.title: One lab, real network
items.text: Both implementations in the same lab measuring across the real Internet.

items.title: Remote labs, two emulators
items.text: Separate labs, each with its own impairment generator configured identically.

items.title: Remote labs, real network
items.text: Separate labs measuring across the real Internet, with no impairment generator.

items.title: Remote labs, one emulator
items.text: Separate labs measuring across the real Internet, with a single impairment generator affecting all flows equally.

viz.caption: HEADER SIZES TO ACCOUNT FOR IN THE TEST SETUP
WHAT TO DOCUMENT FOR EACH IMPLEMENTATION

items.title: Singleton definition
items.text: The single measurement and how the implementation computes it.

items.title: Sample definition
items.text: The set of measurements collected and the conditions under which they are taken.

items.title: Statistics definition
items.text: How the results are summarised, which is what the statistical test compares.

items.title: Timing and synchronization
items.text: The clock requirements the metric depends on and how they are met.

items.title: Options chosen
items.text: Every option the implementation selected, even those not marked MUST or REQUIRED.
